question: Which HTML5 semantic element represents the dominant, unique content of the <body> and should only appear once per page?
explanation: The <main> element specifies the main content of the document, which must be unique and not repeated across pages (like headers/footers).

question: What is the purpose of the 'alt' attribute on an tag in HTML?
options: Provides alternative text for screen readers and when the image fails to load
Specifies image alignment on the page
explanation: The 'alt' attribute provides an alternative textual description for assistive technologies (screen readers) and fallback display.

question: What does the ARIA attribute 'aria-live="polite"' instruct a screen reader to do?
options: Announce updates immediately, interrupting any ongoing speech
Wait until the user is idle before announcing dynamic DOM content changes
Mute all audio feedback on the page
Read content in a lower volume
explanation: aria-live="polite" queues notifications to be spoken when the user finishes their current task, unlike "assertive" which interrupts.

question: Which HTML input type renders a native mobile calendar picker on supported browsers?
explanation: type="date" displays a native date picker dialog formatted to the user's operating system locale.

question: What is the key difference between SVG and HTML5 Canvas?
options: SVG is XML-based vector graphics; Canvas is pixel-based raster bitmap
SVG is raster bitmap; Canvas is vector graphics
Canvas scales infinitely without blur; SVG pixelates
SVG cannot be styled with CSS
explanation: SVG elements are vector nodes retained in the DOM (styleable with CSS), while Canvas draws raster pixels directly into a bitmap buffer.

question: What feature of Web Components encapsulates internal styles and DOM markup from leaking into or being affected by page CSS?
explanation: Shadow DOM provides scoped CSS and isolated DOM trees for web components so styles cannot accidentally conflict.

question: Which meta tag ensures a web page scales properly across mobile viewports?
explanation: The viewport meta tag instructs mobile browsers to render the document at the device's physical pixel width rather than a zoomed-out 980px desktop view.

question: Which HTML tag is used to embed client-side vector icons that can be styled dynamically with CSS fill and stroke?
explanation: Inline <svg> tags become part of the DOM, allowing CSS rules like fill: currentColor and stroke-width to style them directly.

question: What does the 'rel="noopener noreferrer"' attribute on external links (target="_blank") protect against?
options: Reverse tabnabbing where window.opener can redirect the originating tab to a phishing URL
explanation: noopener ensures window.opener is null in the opened page, preventing malicious external sites from hijacking the parent tab.

question: An HTML element can have multiple CSS class names separated by spaces in its 'class' attribute.
explanation: True. class="btn btn-primary active" applies all three class rules to the element.

question: In CSS Flexbox, which property aligns flex items along the cross axis (perpendicular to main axis)?
explanation: justify-content aligns items along the main axis; align-items aligns items along the cross axis.

question: What CSS rule centers a flex child both horizontally and vertically inside its container?
options: display: flex; justify-content: center; align-items: center;
display: flex; text-align: center; margin: auto 0;
display: block; margin: 0 auto; float: center;
explanation: justify-content: center centers on main axis, and align-items: center centers on cross axis.

question: Calculate the specificity score of this CSS selector: 'nav.main-nav ul li a:hover'
explanation: ID count = 0; Classes/pseudo-classes count = 2 (.main-nav, :hover); Tag elements count = 3 (nav, ul, li, a -> actually 4 elements: (0, 2, 4)). Let's check: nav, ul, li, a are 4 elements. Closest standard specificity vector: 0 IDs, 2 classes/attributes, 4 elements.

question: What CSS property specifies whether an element's padding and border are included in its total specified width and height?
explanation: box-sizing: border-box includes padding and border within the declared width/height, preventing layouts from breaking.

question: In CSS Grid, what expression creates responsive columns that wrap automatically without media queries, having minimum width of 250px?
explanation: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(250px, 1fr)) automatically creates as many 250px+ columns as can fit across the row.

question: What new CSS feature introduced in modern browsers allows authoring style precedence layers without relying on selector specificity wars?
explanation: @layer defines explicit priority orders for stylesheets (e.g. @layer reset, base, components, utilities), overriding selector specificity.

question: What is the difference between CSS Container Queries (@container) and Media Queries (@media)?
options: Container queries query the size of a parent component container; Media queries query the browser viewport
Container queries query screen resolution; Media queries query parent width
Container queries only work in Flexbox; Media queries work in Grid
explanation: @container allows a card or component to adapt its layout based on the exact width of its parent container rather than the global viewport.

question: What CSS property defines custom variables in CSS?
explanation: CSS custom properties are prefixed with double dashes: --primary-color: #3b82f6; and accessed via var(--primary-color).

question: Why might a z-index of 9999 fail to display an element above another element with z-index of 1?
options: The element is trapped inside a different Stacking Context with a lower parent z-index
z-index maxes out at 1000 in CSS
explanation: Stacking contexts (created by opacity < 1, transform, filter, will-change, or positioned elements with z-index) contain their children's z-indices.

question: Which CSS pseudo-class matches an element only if it matches a selector passed as an argument (parent selector)?
explanation: The :has() relational pseudo-class acts as a parent/previous sibling selector: e.g., card:has(img) styles a card containing an image.

question: What will `console.log(typeof null)` output in standard JavaScript?
explanation: In JavaScript, typeof null returns 'object'. This is a historical bug in the language's initial 32-bit type tag implementation that cannot be changed for backwards compatibility.
Synchronous code runs first (1, 4). Next, the microtask queue empties (Promise .then prints 3). Finally, the macrotask/timer queue executes (setTimeout prints 2).

question: What is a Closure in JavaScript?
options: A function bundled together with references to its surrounding lexical environment
A method that closes an open network connection
A function that has no return statement
explanation: A closure gives a function access to its outer scope variables even after the outer function has finished executing.

question: How does the 'this' keyword behave inside an arrow function compared to a traditional function declaration?
options: Arrow functions do not bind their own 'this'; they inherit 'this' lexically from the enclosing scope
Arrow functions bind 'this' to the global window/global object strictly
Arrow functions can be rebound using .bind() or .call()
Arrow functions bind 'this' to the DOM element that fired the event
explanation: Arrow functions lack their own 'this' binding and lexically resolve 'this' from the enclosing execution context.

question: What does `Promise.allSettled(promises)` return compared to `Promise.all(promises)`?
options: Waits for all promises to settle (fulfill or reject) and returns an array of status objects without short-circuiting on rejection
Rejects immediately if any single promise rejects
Returns only the first promise that resolves
Cancels any ongoing promises after 5 seconds
explanation: Promise.all rejects on the first failure, while Promise.allSettled waits for all promises to finish and returns their outcomes.

question: What is the difference between '==' and '===' in JavaScript?
options: '==' performs type coercion before comparison; '===' checks both value and type without coercion
Both operators behave identically in ES6+
'==' is used only for comparing objects
explanation: The strict equality operator (===) checks value and type without converting types; loose equality (==) coerces types (e.g. 0 == '0' is true, 0 === '0' is false).

question: What does the Optional Chaining operator (?.) do in JavaScript?
options: Safely accesses nested object properties without throwing a TypeError if an intermediate reference is null or undefined
Creates a conditional ternary expression in one symbol
Checks if an array is non-empty
explanation: user?.profile?.avatar short-circuits and evaluates to undefined rather than throwing 'Cannot read properties of undefined'.

question: What is the Nullish Coalescing operator (??) in JavaScript?
options: A logical operator that returns its right-hand operand only when its left-hand operand is null or undefined
An operator that treats 0 and empty string '' as falsy and returns the right operand
explanation: Unlike || which falls back on any falsy value (including 0, false, ''), ?? only falls back if the left operand is strictly null or undefined.

question: What is a WeakMap in JavaScript, and how does it prevent memory leaks?
options: Keys must be objects, and keys are held weakly allowing them to be garbage collected if no other references exist
Keys can only be strings that expire after a timeout
Values cannot be overwritten once set
It is an array that automatically truncates its size
explanation: In WeakMap, keys are weakly held object references. When an object key has no other references in memory, it is automatically garbage-collected.

question: What JavaScript method creates a deep copy of a standard serializable object in modern browsers without external libraries?
explanation: structuredClone() is a standard web API that recursively copies nested objects, arrays, Dates, Maps, Sets, and circular references.

question: In DOM Event Propagation, what are the three sequential phases of an event?
options: Capturing Phase, Target Phase, Bubbling Phase
Target Phase, Bubbling Phase, Capturing Phase
Bubbling Phase, Processing Phase, Dispatch Phase
Initialization Phase, Execution Phase, Destruction Phase
explanation: Events travel down from Window to target (Capturing), trigger on the target element (Target), and bubble back up to Window (Bubbling).

question: What is Event Delegation in JavaScript DOM programming?
options: Attaching a single event listener to a common ancestor instead of separate listeners on dozens of child elements
Delegating event handling to a background Web Worker
explanation: Event delegation leverages event bubbling to handle clicks on current and future child elements using event.target on a parent listener.

question: What is the difference between `event.preventDefault()` and `event.stopPropagation()`?
options: preventDefault cancels the browser's default action (e.g. following a link); stopPropagation stops the event from bubbling up the DOM tree
stopPropagation cancels default actions; preventDefault stops bubbling
Both methods do the exact same thing
explanation: preventDefault halts native browser behavior (submitting form, navigating anchor), while stopPropagation prevents parent handlers from catching the event.

question: What browser API allows asynchronously monitoring when a DOM element enters or exits the viewport (e.g. for lazy-loading images)?
explanation: IntersectionObserver efficiently detects when target elements intersect with an ancestor or top-level document viewport without scroll event lag.

question: What browser storage mechanism persists data across browser tabs and sessions until explicitly cleared by user or code, with roughly 5-10MB capacity?
explanation: localStorage persists across browser restarts and all tabs of the same origin. sessionStorage is cleared when the tab closes.

question: What cookie attribute prevents client-side JavaScript (`document.cookie`) from accessing the cookie, mitigating XSS token theft?
explanation: The HttpOnly flag ensures that cookies can only be sent over HTTP requests and cannot be read via JavaScript document.cookie.

question: What triggers a browser 'Reflow' (Layout calculation) versus a mere 'Repaint'?
options: Reflow recalculates geometry and positions of elements (e.g. offsetWidth, changing width/height); Repaint updates visual pixels (e.g. background-color)
Reflow only changes colors; Repaint changes element sizes
Both are identical operations in the browser engine
explanation: Reflow is computationally expensive because changing geometry forces the browser to recalculate bounding boxes for the affected branch.

question: What is a CORS preflight request, and which HTTP method does the browser issue for it?
options: An automated OPTIONS request sent before non-simple cross-origin requests to check server permissions
A GET request with custom headers
A HEAD request to check content length
explanation: Browsers send an HTTP OPTIONS preflight request before complex requests (like PUT, DELETE, or custom headers) to verify Access-Control headers.

question: What browser feature runs JavaScript scripts in background threads isolated from the main thread DOM?
explanation: Web Workers execute heavy calculations in a separate background thread, communicating with the main thread via postMessage without freezing the UI.

question: What technique delays function execution until a specified delay has elapsed since the last time the function was invoked (e.g., search input)?
explanation: Debouncing groups rapid successive calls into a single invocation after quiet time, whereas throttling enforces a max execution rate.

question: Why must React component state updates not mutate state directly (e.g., state.count = 5)?
options: React relies on object reference equality to detect changes and schedule component re-renders
Direct mutation crashes the V8 engine
State variables are frozen with Object.freeze automatically
Direct mutation only works in production builds
explanation: React components re-render when state changes; mutating existing objects keeps the same memory address, bypassing shallow equality checks.

question: What does the second argument (dependency array) in React's `useEffect(fn, deps)` control?
options: Specifies which state/prop values cause the effect function to re-run when changed
explanation: An empty array [] runs the effect once on mount; specifying [a, b] runs the effect whenever a or b changes.

question: What is the primary difference between `useMemo` and `useCallback` in React?
options: `useMemo` caches the calculated result of a function; `useCallback` caches the function definition itself
`useMemo` is for class components; `useCallback` is for function components
explanation: useMemo(() => computeValue(a, b), [a, b]) returns a memoized value; useCallback(fn, deps) returns a memoized function reference.

question: Why should you never use the array index as a 'key' prop for dynamic lists that can be reordered, sorted, or filtered in React?
options: Index keys confuse React's reconciliation diffing, causing component state or form input values to attach to the wrong elements
Index keys cause syntax errors in JSX
explanation: When list items reorder or delete, their indices change, misleading React's diffing algorithm and causing subtle UI bugs.

question: What does the `useRef` hook return in React?
options: A mutable object with a '.current' property that persists across renders without triggering a re-render when mutated
A read-only snapshot of component props
explanation: useRef returns { current: initialValue }. Changing ref.current does not cause the component to re-render, making it ideal for DOM nodes and timer IDs.

question: What was the primary goal of the React Fiber architecture rewrite?
options: To enable incremental rendering by splitting rendering work into chunks across animation frames and pausing/prioritizing updates
To eliminate the Virtual DOM entirely
To force static typing across all JSX components
explanation: React Fiber turned the recursive stack reconciler into an incremental linked-list tree where work can be paused, aborted, or prioritized.

question: What hook in React is designed to read layout from the DOM and synchronously re-render before the browser paints screen pixels?
explanation: useLayoutEffect fires synchronously after all DOM mutations but before the browser paints, preventing visual flickers when measuring DOM elements.

question: What is a 'controlled component' in React form handling?
options: An input element whose value is driven by React state and updated via an onChange handler
A component that cannot be edited by the user
A component rendered on the server
An input using ref to read value on submit
explanation: In a controlled component, form data is handled by a React component via value={state} and onChange={e => setState(e.target.value)}.

question: What does React 18's `useTransition` hook allow developers to do?
options: Mark non-urgent UI state updates as transitions that can be interrupted by higher-priority urgent updates (like typing)
Transition between page routes in Next.js
explanation: startTransition allows updates to be deprioritized so heavy renders don't block immediate user input like keypresses and clicks.

question: What is the purpose of React Error Boundaries?
options: Catch JavaScript errors anywhere in their child component tree, log those errors, and display a fallback UI instead of crashing the whole app
Catch compile-time syntax errors in Babel
explanation: Class components implementing componentDidCatch or static getDerivedStateFromError catch render-phase crashes and render fallback UI.

question: What is the key difference between TypeScript `interface` and `type` alias?
options: Interfaces can be merged via declaration merging; type aliases cannot and can define unions/primitives
Type aliases cannot define object shapes
Interfaces compile to JavaScript functions; type aliases are deleted
There is no difference in TypeScript
explanation: Multiple interface declarations with the same name merge their properties, while type aliases support unions (type X = A | B) and mapped types.

question: In TypeScript, what does the utility type `Partial<T>` do?
options: Constructs a type with all properties of T set to optional (?)
Extracts only primitive properties from T
explanation: Partial<T> wraps every property of type T in optional: { [P in keyof T]?: T[P] }.

question: In TypeScript, what does the utility type `Record<K, T>` construct?
options: An object type whose property keys are K and property values are T
explanation: Record<string, number> defines an object whose keys are strings and values are numbers.

question: What is the purpose of the 'unknown' type in TypeScript versus 'any'?
options: 'unknown' is type-safe; you must perform type checking or casting before performing operations on an unknown variable
'unknown' can only accept null or undefined
'unknown' is converted to number at runtime
explanation: 'any' turns off type checking completely, whereas 'unknown' forces the developer to narrow the type via typeof, instanceof, or type guards.

question: What TypeScript keyword is used to extract the return type of a function type inside a conditional type?
explanation: type ReturnType<T> = T extends (...args: any[]) => infer R ? R : any; uses 'infer' to deduce the return type variable R.

question: What does the 'defer' attribute on an external `<script src="app.js" defer></script>` tag do?
options: Downloads the script in parallel and executes it only after HTML parsing is completely finished
Executes the script immediately, blocking HTML parsing
Delays downloading until the user scrolls
Loads the script inside an iframe
explanation: defer scripts download in the background without blocking the parser and execute in document order right before DOMContentLoaded.

question: What is the difference between 'async' and 'defer' attributes on script tags?
options: 'async' executes as soon as it downloads, potentially out of order; 'defer' executes after HTML parsing in document order
'defer' executes immediately; 'async' waits for document complete
'async' only works for CSS; 'defer' is for JS
explanation: async scripts execute the moment they finish downloading, interrupting parsing; defer scripts execute orderly after DOM parsing completes.

question: What Core Web Vital metric measures visual stability and unexpected layout shifts on a page?
explanation: CLS measures unexpected shifts in visual elements as content loads, aiming for a score under 0.1 for good user experience.

question: What Core Web Vital replaced First Input Delay (FID) to assess page responsiveness to user interactions?
explanation: INP observes the latency of all click, tap, and keyboard interactions throughout the entire page lifecycle.

question: Which HTTP header instructs the browser to enforce HTTPS connections exclusively for a domain?
explanation: HSTS tells browsers to convert all insecure http:// requests to https:// automatically before network transmission.

question: What security header helps prevent Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) and data injection attacks by restricting resource loading domains?
explanation: CSP restricts which scripts, styles, images, and endpoints can be executed or loaded by the browser.

question: In CSS, what does the unit 'rem' stand for?
explanation: 1rem equals the font-size of the root <html> element (typically 16px by default).

question: What is the difference between 'rem' and 'em' units in CSS?
options: 'rem' is relative to the root <html> font-size; 'em' is relative to the immediate parent element's font-size
'em' is relative to root; 'rem' is relative to parent
'rem' only applies to margins; 'em' applies to padding
They are identical in modern CSS
explanation: em compounds based on the cascade of parent font-sizes, whereas rem remains consistently anchored to the root element.

question: What CSS property creates a frosted-glass blur effect on content behind an element?
explanation: backdrop-filter applies graphic effects (like blur or saturate) to the area behind an element with semi-transparent background.

question: In JavaScript, what does `Object.freeze(obj)` do?
options: Prevents adding new properties, removing existing properties, or modifying values of existing properties (shallow)
Clones the object into an immutable Proxy
Deeply freezes all nested objects automatically
explanation: Object.freeze makes an object shallowly immutable; properties cannot be added, removed, or changed.

question: What is the difference between Array.prototype.map() and Array.prototype.forEach()?
options: map() returns a new array with transformed elements; forEach() executes a side effect and returns undefined
forEach() returns a new array; map() returns undefined
explanation: map creates and returns a new array with the return value of each callback call; forEach returns undefined.

question: What does Array.prototype.reduce() do in JavaScript?
options: Executes a reducer callback on each array element to accumulate them into a single resultant value
Shrinks the array length by half
explanation: reduce runs an accumulator function across all elements, producing a single combined result (sum, object map, etc.).

question: How do you remove duplicates from a JavaScript array `arr` in a single line using ES6?
explanation: Sets only store unique values, so [...new Set(arr)] or Array.from(new Set(arr)) discards duplicates.

question: What is the purpose of the 'Symbol' primitive data type introduced in ES6?
options: Creates completely unique, immutable identifiers often used as non-enumerable object property keys
explanation: Every Symbol() call produces a unique value that cannot clash with other keys, even if initialized with identical descriptions.

question: What JavaScript metaprogramming object allows intercepting and customizing operations like property lookups, assignments, and function calls?
explanation: new Proxy(target, handler) intercepts fundamental operations (traps like get, set, has, deleteProperty) to customize behavior.

question: What HTTP response status code signifies '204 No Content'?
options: The request succeeded, but the server has no response body to return
The server failed to locate the resource
explanation: 204 indicates successful request completion without returning a message body (often used in DELETE or PUT operations).

question: What is tree-shaking in modern JavaScript bundlers (Vite, Rollup, Webpack)?
options: Dead code elimination that analyzes ES module imports/exports to discard unused code from the production bundle
explanation: Tree-shaking statically analyzes ES import/export graphs to strip out exported functions that are never imported or called.

question: What is the CSS pseudo-class for styling an element when it receives keyboard focus, avoiding outline styling on mouse clicks?
explanation: :focus-visible only applies focus indicators when navigation is initiated via keyboard (e.g. Tab key) rather than pointer clicks.

question: What does CSS `pointer-events: none` do to an element?
options: Makes the element non-targetable for click, hover, and drag events, passing events through to underlying elements
explanation: pointer-events: none causes mouse and pointer events to ignore the element and trigger on whatever is visually beneath it.

question: What is the difference between `display: none` and `visibility: hidden` in CSS?
options: `display: none` removes the element from the document layout flow; `visibility: hidden` hides it while preserving its physical layout space
`visibility: hidden` removes it from layout flow; `display: none` preserves space
Both free the layout space equally
Only `display: none` hides text from screen readers
explanation: display: none collapses the element so it occupies 0px in layout. visibility: hidden keeps the element's box in the DOM layout intact.

question: What is the 'SameSite' cookie attribute option that prevents the cookie from being sent in all cross-site requests, including top-level navigations?
explanation: SameSite=Strict withholds cookies on all cross-origin requests, including when clicking a normal hyperlink from an external domain.

question: What lifecycle event fires when the HTML document has been completely parsed and DOM tree built, without waiting for stylesheets or images?
explanation: DOMContentLoaded fires as soon as HTML is parsed into the DOM. The window 'load' event waits for all external resources (images, styles).

question: What method stops an active `setInterval` timer in JavaScript?
explanation: clearInterval takes the ID returned by setInterval and stops further scheduled recurring invocations.

question: What CSS property optimizes performance by informing the browser ahead of time which properties on an element are expected to change?
explanation: will-change: transform, opacity allows the browser to promote the element to its own GPU compositor layer before animation begins.

question: Which of the following is a pure function in JavaScript?
explanation: A pure function always returns the exact same output for the same arguments and produces zero observable side effects.

question: What is JSX in React development?
options: A syntax extension for JavaScript that resembles HTML and compiles to React.createElement function calls
A separate programming language compiled to WebAssembly
A database query syntax for GraphQL
A JSON format for CSS styles
explanation: JSX provides HTML-like syntax inside JavaScript, which compilers like Babel or SWC transform into React.createElement / jsx runtime calls.

question: In React, what is 'prop drilling'?
options: The process of passing props through multiple levels of intermediate components that do not need the data themselves
explanation: Prop drilling occurs when state must be passed down a deep component hierarchy, solved by React Context or state management stores.

question: What is the purpose of the React Context API?
options: Provides a way to share values between components without having to explicitly pass a prop through every level of the tree
explanation: React Context allows sharing global-like state (themes, authentication, locale) across an entire subtree.

question: What happens when you call a state updater function in React with a callback: `setCount(prev => prev + 1)`?
options: React passes the most recent guaranteed state value into the callback, avoiding stale closure race conditions in async operations
It runs the state update in a web worker
It executes synchronously before the next line of code
It resets the state to 0 first
explanation: Functional state updates guarantee access to the current pending state rather than capturing stale values from old render closures.

question: What is Server-Side Rendering (SSR) in modern web frameworks like Next.js or Nuxt?
options: Generating full HTML markup for a page on the server per request, sending rendered HTML to the client for faster initial paint and SEO
Executing JavaScript exclusively on user's GPU
Compiling client code into a single desktop binary
explanation: SSR renders the component tree into HTML on the server, speeding up FCP/LCP and making pages immediately indexable by web crawlers.

question: What is 'Hydration' in modern SSR frameworks?
options: Attaching event listeners and client React state to server-rendered static HTML markup to make it interactive
Cleaning memory leaks in the browser
Pre-fetching all images on the page
explanation: Hydration bridges the gap between static HTML generated by the server and dynamic client-side React event handlers.

question: What is the Fetch API return type in JavaScript?
options: A Promise that resolves to a Response object
explanation: fetch(url) returns a Promise resolving to a Response object representing the HTTP response, which requires .json() or .text() to parse.

question: Why does `fetch()` NOT reject its promise on HTTP 404 or 500 status codes?
options: A Promise from fetch() only rejects on network failures or CORS errors; HTTP 4xx/5xx are considered successful HTTP communications with response.ok = false
Because 404 is an informational status code
It is a bug in the Fetch spec that cannot be fixed
Because only POST requests can reject
explanation: fetch only rejects if the network fails or request is blocked. 404 and 500 still represent completed HTTP exchanges, check response.ok.

question: How can you abort an in-flight `fetch()` request in JavaScript?
options: Using an AbortController instance and passing its signal to the fetch options: { signal: controller.signal }
explanation: const controller = new AbortController(); fetch(url, { signal: controller.signal }); controller.abort(); cleanly cancels ongoing HTTP requests.

question: What is the CSS clamp() function used for?
options: Clamping a value between an allowable minimum, preferred, and maximum value: clamp(min, preferred, max)
Fixing an element to screen viewport
explanation: clamp(1rem, 2.5vw, 2rem) creates fluid typography and dimensions that dynamically adapt to viewport size within strict bounds.

question: What CSS property prevents text from wrapping onto a new line?
explanation: white-space: nowrap prevents text sequences from breaking onto multiple lines.

question: How do you truncate overflow text with an ellipsis (...) in CSS?
options: overflow: hidden; white-space: nowrap; text-overflow: ellipsis;
explanation: The combination of overflow: hidden, white-space: nowrap, and text-overflow: ellipsis renders standard three-dot overflow truncation.

question: What is the difference between `null` and `undefined` in JavaScript?
options: `undefined` means a variable has been declared but not assigned a value; `null` represents an intentional assignment of an empty value
`null` is a type of number; `undefined` is an object
They are identical in every context
explanation: undefined indicates absence of value by default in uninitialized variables or missing parameters; null indicates explicit absence set by program logic.

question: What does the JavaScript spread operator `...` do when applied to an array `[1, 2, ...arr]`?
options: Expands the iterable array elements into individual elements
Converts the array to a JSON string
explanation: Spread syntax expands iterable items (arrays, strings, sets) in place into expressions or function argument lists.

question: What is a 'polyfill' in web development?
options: A piece of code used to provide modern web functionality on older browsers that do not natively support it
explanation: Polyfills emulate newer APIs (e.g. Promise, fetch, Array.prototype.flat) on legacy browser engines using backward-compatible code.

question: Which CSS property specifies how image or video content should resize to fit its container box?
explanation: object-fit: cover scales the media to maintain aspect ratio while filling the element box, clipping overflow.

question: What does the CSS property `aspect-ratio: 16 / 9;` achieve?
options: Maintains a 16:9 proportional ratio between element width and height automatically without padding hacks
Sets width to 16px and height to 9px
explanation: aspect-ratio allows setting explicit proportions, preventing layout shift while responsive images load.

question: In Web Performance, what is 'Code Splitting'?
options: Splitting application JavaScript bundles into smaller chunks that can be loaded dynamically on demand using dynamic import()
Dividing frontend and backend code into separate Git repositories
Running code across multiple CPU threads
explanation: Code splitting ensures users only download the code needed for their current route or interaction, dramatically cutting initial bundle payload.

question: What is the difference between client-side routing (Single Page Application) and traditional multi-page navigation?
options: Client-side routing intercepts anchor clicks and updates the view via JavaScript History API without reloading the entire page
Client-side routing requires reloading HTML on every link click
Client-side routing cannot update the browser URL bar
Client-side routing only works over WebSockets
explanation: SPAs use history.pushState() to update the URL and render new component views client-side without full-page server round-trips.

question: What is a Progressive Web App (PWA) Service Worker lifecycle event that allows caching app shell assets offline?
options: 'install' event (caches static assets using the CacheStorage API)
explanation: During the Service Worker 'install' event, event.waitUntil() caches essential HTML, CSS, and JS files into CacheStorage for offline resilience.
